Rebels and Their Redeemer
Tim Cochrell | September 13, 2026
Isaiah 1:1-31 | pg. 530 of the Auditorium Bibles
Main Idea: God convicts us so that he can comfort us. He exposes our
delusions of self-sufficiency so that we will turn from our sin and turn to him for
salvation.
Introducing Isaiah (v.1): Isaiah’s name means “The Lord Saves.” His prophetic
ministry directly addresses our problem and God’s provision.
Rebellion (v.2-9)
A. Confrontation: Sin deceives our hearts and distorts our perspective. The first
step in salvation is a recognition of our true condition.
B. Accusation:
They are stubborn and senseless, forgetting God’s faithful care.
They are proud and polluted, forsaking God who satisfies.
They are desperate and desolate, but think they can save themselves.
C. Glimpse of Grace: Their rebellion deserves God’s destruction, but God offers
salvation because of his mercy.
Repentance (v.10-20): When convicted of sin, we can either conceal it or
confess it. One compounds our guilt; the other cleanses it.
A. Conceal: God is disgusted by worship that is hollow and hypocritical. He
hates every form of worship that does not flow from a heart of humility and
repentance.
B. Confess: God’s accusation is followed by an invitation to repent. He calls us
to honestly confess and urgently forsake our sin.
Redemption (v.21-31)
A. Sobering Reflection: God uses shocking language to awaken them to the
severity of their condition and the stubbornness of their pride.
B. Stunning Redemption: God will punish them in order to purify them. He will
redeem and restore hopeless sinners through his justice and by his grace.
C. Stubborn Refusal: Those who resist conviction and refuse salvation will be
objects of God’s judgment rather than recipients of his grace.
